sections.h2: Where do I search official property records in Volusia County?
sections.html:
Start with two sites: the Clerk of the Circuit Court for recorded documents and the Property Appraiser for parcels. The clerk's Official Records inquiry holds the index and images of recorded documents from April 4, 1988 to the present. It lists deeds, mortgages, judgments, marriages, divorces, powers of attorney and probate filings. Only released records appear online, meaning they have been recorded, indexed, verified and cleared for public viewing, so a very recent filing may be missing.

The Volusia County Property Appraiser's search page offers several tools, including searches by name, address or alternate key, an advanced search by fields and ranges, a personal property search, a sales search and a map search. Real property results can be exported to CSV. Use the clerk for what was recorded against a parcel and the appraiser for what the parcel is, who the tax roll shows as owner and what has sold nearby.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a deed in Volusia County?
sections.html:
The clerk's deed checklist prices the recording itself at $10.00 for the first page up to 8.5 by 14 inches, and $8.50 for each additional page. Indexing more than four names adds $1.00 for each extra name. The state documentary stamp tax on a deed is separate, at 70 cents per $100 of consideration or fraction of it.

The checklist says the tax applies to the full consideration, and a mortgage's value may not be subtracted. A nominal-consideration recital such as ten dollars and other valuable considerations still triggers the minimum tax. Florida makes every party to the deed liable for the tax, whichever side agrees to pay.

sections.h2: What must a deed include before the Volusia County clerk records it?
sections.html:
The clerk requires an original document with a clear layout and specific details printed on it. A copy will not be accepted. The recording checklist spells out the requirements.

  • A blank 3-inch by 3-inch square at the top right corner of the first page for office use.
  • The legal description of the land and the parcel identification number.
  • Each signer's name printed beneath the signature, with a post office address.
  • The grantee's name and post office address, except on a mortgage.
  • The name and address of the person who prepared the instrument.
  • Two subscribing witnesses, each with a printed name and address.
  • A notary certificate that meets Florida notary requirements.

Florida law separately requires a deed to be signed before two subscribing witnesses and allows witnessing by audio-video technology. The clerk notes that other statutes may affect whether a specific transfer is valid, and suggests asking an attorney about unusual transfers. Checks go to the Clerk of the Circuit Court.

sections.h2: Where and how can I submit documents for recording in Volusia County?
sections.html:
You can record in person at the DeLand courthouse, drop off in Daytona Beach, mail documents, or e-record through a vendor. In DeLand, the Recording Department is at the Volusia County Courthouse, Room A121, 101 N. Alabama Avenue, and the clerk says documents are recorded and returned while you wait. The clerk's phone for recording questions is 386-736-5912.

  • Daytona Beach drop box: Courthouse Annex, 125 East Orange Avenue, picked up each business day at 7:00 a.m. with no promise of same-day recording. Include a cover sheet, the original and payment.
  • Mail: Volusia County Clerk of the Circuit Court, Attention Recording Department, P.O. Box 6043, DeLand, FL 32721, with a self-addressed stamped envelope.
  • E-recording vendors named by the clerk: Simplifile, CSC, ePN and Hopdox.

The clerk calls e-recording faster and cheaper than paper. Mailed payment can be a check, money order, business check or cashier's check made out to the Clerk of the Circuit Court.

sections.h2: How do I find a parcel or sales history through the Volusia County Property Appraiser?
sections.html:
Use the appraiser's real property search by name, address or alternate key, then open the parcel for detail. The sales search narrows by select fields and ranges, which helps when you want to see what nearby homes sold for before pricing your own. A map search shows parcel details on an interactive map.

The Property Appraiser is also where homestead and other exemption questions go, with March 1 as the filing deadline set by state law. After a sale, the next January 1 assessment reflects the new owner and a reset value, which is why buyers should expect a different bill than the seller paid.

sections.h2: What other filings does the Volusia County clerk handle on property?
sections.html:
The clerk's records cover several property events that a seller may meet, and each has its own search or report on clerk.org. Check them early, because a filing against the parcel can shape how and when you can sell.

The clerk's records cover several property events that a seller may meet. Weekly foreclosure reports list new foreclosure suits in circuit and county cases, and each stays available for about 30 days. Tax deed information shows properties up for the next courthouse tax deed auction, and a Lands Available for Taxes list shows land that drew no bidders.

For a judicial foreclosure, the clerk's fee page lists a $70.00 charge to conduct the sale and issue and record the title. State law sets the sale between 20 and 35 days after judgment unless the plaintiff agrees to more, with a 5 percent deposit from the high bidder and a 10 day window for objections. If the sale produces surplus funds, the owner should check with the clerk within 10 days.

sections.h2: What should a Volusia County seller check in the records before closing?
sections.html:
Pull the owner's chain of title, open mortgages, liens and judgments in the clerk's Official Records, and compare the legal description and parcel number to the appraiser's record. Any mismatch is worth fixing before you sign. Also check for open foreclosure or tax deed activity against the parcel.

The clerk also publishes a daily list of new suits filed in circuit and county cases, which stays available for about 30 days, and a monthly probate report that requires subscriber access. Neither replaces a title search, but they show whether a case has been filed against a parcel or an estate.

If you inherited the home, probate filings also appear among the official records the clerk indexes. When taxes or liens are past due, ask the Volusia County tax collector for a payoff, and have your closing agent confirm the payoff before you accept an offer from any buyer.

faqs.q: How much does the Volusia County clerk charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: The checklist lists $10.00 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page, plus $1.00 for each name beyond four. Documentary stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 of consideration is separate.

faqs.q: How far back do Volusia County online official records go?
faqs.a: The clerk's Official Records inquiry covers recorded documents from April 4, 1988 to the present. Only released records appear, so very recent filings may not be visible yet.

faqs.q: Can I mail a deed to the Volusia County clerk?
faqs.a: Yes. Mail the original, not a copy, with payment and a self-addressed stamped envelope to P.O. Box 6043, DeLand, FL 32721, Attention Recording Department.

faqs.q: Does Volusia County accept electronic recording?
faqs.a: Yes. The clerk lists Simplifile, Corporate Service Company, eRecording Partners Network and Hopdox as e-recording vendors, and says e-recording is faster and less expensive.

faqs.q: How many witnesses does a Volusia County deed need?
faqs.a: Two subscribing witnesses, each with a printed name and address, per the clerk's checklist and Florida's deed statute. Check with the clerk's recording office at 386-736-5912 if a document is unusual.
